figures.caption: Learning inertial odometry without velocity or position labels across six datasets. Models are trained separately from scratch. With a reference attitude for teacher gravity compensation, our models refined by pose graph distillation (PGD, red) have an average velocity error within $0.07$ m/s of the same-architecture supervised AirIO† baseline (blue).
figures.headline: Models trained without velocity or position labels reach average velocity error within 0.07 m/s of the supervised AirIO† baseline across six datasets.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Integration Self-Supervision trains the motion network to match the body-frame velocity change predicted by the frozen integration teacher under a squared velocity-change loss, supervising only the velocity mean. Pose Graph Distillation (PGD) builds a full-sequence pose graph from the teacher’s IMU factors and the network’s velocity factors. The graph posterior $\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{opt}}$ then supervises the network through an L2 loss. Velocity Regularization, $\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{reg}}$, is used over detected static frames.
figures.headline: Integration self-supervision matches the network's velocity change to a frozen teacher, and pose graph distillation then refines it.

abstract: Learning inertial odometry for a new platform usually requires ground-truth trajectories. We show that an inertial odometry model can instead be trained from scratch by a myopic teacher that integrates the IMU over each short window independently, a scheme we call integration self-supervision. Interestingly, although supervised only by short-window velocity changes, the student learns to directly predict velocity, and does so more accurately than its integration teacher. Pose graph distillation then refines the model with sequence-consistent targets from a pose graph over many windows. Training on a new platform therefore no longer requires collecting ground-truth trajectories, but only calibrating the IMU and recording data during normal operation. Across six datasets spanning pedestrians, drones, quadrupeds, and a humanoid, the same recipe with no velocity or position labels trains models that come within $0.07$ m/s average velocity error of a same-architecture supervised baseline.

sections.body: Inertial odometry drifts because double integration accumulates IMU noise and bias. Existing learned methods need pose- or velocity-labeled trajectories, which tie the model to one embodiment and make adaptation costly. The paper proposes integration self-supervision: a student is trained so that its predicted endpoint velocities differ by the body-frame velocity change that a myopic integration teacher computes over each short window. The authors report that the student learns repeated motion patterns and exceeds the teacher over long horizons. Pose graph distillation then refines it using sequence-level targets. The authors state that self-supervised training approaches the supervised baseline on six datasets.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Inertial odometry can be trained on each new platform from its unlabeled IMU data, without ground-truth trajectories.

sections.body: Learned inertial odometry systems such as IONet, RIDI, RoNIN, and TLIO fit velocity from labeled sequences. Prior self-supervised methods either borrow a second sensor such as stereo cameras, LiDAR, or photometric consistency, or use rotation equivariance, which still fits the motion prior from labels. Imperative model predictive control relies on a known dynamics model of the platform. Multi-IMU legged filters such as MIPO and DogLegs use leg kinematics. The paper states that its method needs neither an additional sensor nor such a prior, because the IMU integrator itself supplies the training target.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Earlier self-supervised inertial methods need an extra sensor, a labeled prior, or a known dynamics model; this one needs none of them.

sections.body: The network takes raw accelerometer and gyroscope measurements in a window of W samples and predicts body-frame velocity. It is based on AirIO with the attitude encoder removed, denoted AirIO†. Integration self-supervision integrates the IMU over each window after subtracting biases estimated from static frames, and trains the difference of predicted endpoint velocities to match the integrated change. A regularization loss on IMU-detected static frames limits drift. Pose graph distillation then optimizes velocities jointly over many windows with Gauss–Newton and fine-tunes the network on the resulting targets. Per Table II, removing the attitude encoder costs AirIO† less than 0.05 m/s in average velocity error relative to AirIO.
sections.heading: Self-Supervised Inertial Odometry
sections.headline: Integration self-supervision matches each window's IMU-integrated velocity change, and pose graph distillation then refines the network.

sections.body: Experiments cover six datasets: TLIO, EuRoC, Blackbird, MIPO, GrandTour, and a Unitree G1 humanoid set. Metrics are average velocity error (AVE) in body-frame velocity and absolute trajectory error (ATE) after rigid alignment, with learned trajectories integrated from ground-truth orientation. With the reference-attitude teacher and pose graph distillation, the AVE gap to AirIO† stays below 0.07 m/s on every dataset. Pose graph distillation lowers AVE by 4–11% on five datasets; on GrandTour the change is 0.096 to 0.095 m/s. ATE rises on EuRoC from 9.03 to 10.23 m. On MIPO, the proprioceptive student reaches 0.146 m/s, against 0.199 m/s for the model-based filter.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Self-supervised models stay within 0.07 m/s average velocity error of the supervised baseline on all six datasets.

sections.body: The student is compared with its integration teacher across evaluation horizons, trained on TLIO. At 20 s, the model trained with the longest supervision window reaches approximately 0.14 m/s error against the teacher's 0.89 m/s, which the text calls roughly sixfold. The teacher is more accurate over short horizons, while the student's error grows more slowly. Models evaluated on other datasets without retraining have at least 1.9× and up to 34× the AVE of the model trained on the evaluation dataset. Held-out AVE on TLIO improves monotonically with more unlabeled data. The authors note that these transfer results do not separate embodiment effects from differences in sensors, calibration, or motion distributions.
sections.heading: Analysis of the Learned Velocity Model
sections.headline: The student's long-horizon velocity-change error stays below its integration teacher's, and it transfers poorly across datasets.

sections.body: Self-supervision needs enough motion excitation in the training data and a corrected IMU bias. Zero-mean noise with standard deviation up to 0.5 m/s² raises AVE by at most 9%. A constant bias of 0.1 m/s² raises AVE by 39%, and 0.5 m/s² more than quadruples it. A tilt error leaks gravity into the targets: a gyroscope-integrated attitude raises AVE by 22% on TLIO, and the onboard AHRS raises it by 29% on MIPO. Repeating pose graph distillation on the self-supervised network raises AVE from 0.095 to 0.202 m/s over 80 iterations. The from-scratch IMU-only run diverges after about 300 iterations. The authors state that better bias calibration or a gravity-aided filter would narrow the tilt gap, but these are outside the paper's scope.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Constant IMU bias degrades training far more than zero-mean noise does, so bias must be corrected before training.

sections.body: The conclusion draws two lessons. First, learned inertial odometry needs only a calibrated IMU and the platform's own unlabeled recordings. Second, a myopic teacher can train a student more accurate than itself. The authors argue that averaging noisy increments explains why the student can surpass the teacher, but not why matching velocity changes yields a motion model rather than an integrator; that point rests on empirical evidence. Which motion properties make an embodiment learnable from noisy increments, and how much unlabeled data this requires, are listed as open questions. A theoretical account of the mechanism is named as the main direction for future work.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The student's motion model comes from averaging noisy increments, though the paper offers empirical rather than theoretical evidence for why.

sections.body: The appendix gives the covariance propagation matrices behind the uncertainty that weights integration factors in pose graph distillation, followed by training details. Table VI lists supervision horizons of 5.12 s for TLIO, 3.65 s for GrandTour, and 0.41 s for MIPO. Pose graph distillation uses one outer round, Gauss–Newton with at most 10 iterations, and windows of 1024 samples. Appendix C describes a block-sparse solver. Table VII reports a 1.8× speedup at N=128. It states that the dense solver exceeds device memory for N≥512 on a 32 GB GPU, while the sparse solver solves N=1024 in under half a second. The appendix also includes sample trajectories for five datasets.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix covers covariance propagation, training configurations, pose graph solver implementation with timing, and sample trajectories.
